MIDWEST SAFETY: Uncover. Inform. Empower.

Please consider JOINING for $1 a month. It *really* helps us do original reporting like this. 

MERCH! Midwest-Safety.com

CONTACT US:
Complaints? Video submissions? Tips? Sponsorships? Collabs? Business inquires? 
Email our board at mn.safety.alerts@gmail.com. 

BE NICE:
The individuals presented in these videos may be suffering from the effects of alcohol, drug abuse, a mental health disorder or simply having a bad day. The videos should NOT be presumed to be representative of their general behavior. Everyone deserves to be treated with respect.

Shane also detailed his relationship with Tammy. Flagler deputies caught Shane less than 24 hours after he entered the county, an example of their efficiency, but not without controversy. The pursuit was unauthorized, and officers sped it over twice the limit without lights or sirens. lights or sirens, frustrating some civilians. In their own footage release, FCSO edited out radio traffic about the unauthorized chase. Conservative statistics cite that police pursuit fatalities happen almost daily in the U.S. and often involve bystanders. The San Francisco Chronicle provides some of the best resources regarding these statistics with an interactive website that details some of the most dangerous states for police pursuit fatalities from 2017 to to 2022. Georgia and Alabama takes the top two spots with over 20 deaths per one million people, accounting for 10% of pursuit deaths in the whole nation. Florida, where this video takes place, falls into 34th. Most pursuits in the U.S., regardless of the outcome, are subject to review by the agency, and officers can receive coachings or discipline if found violating policy. Looking at the 2017 Flagler Vehicle Apprehension Policy, this certainly seems to be the case, But this information is not publicly accessible. It is worth noting, however, that stolen vehicles of this nature tend to be used in more serious crimes. Had officers not continued to apprehend, there would be plenty of critics upset with law enforcement if the suspects committed a more serious crime after getting away. This time, the risk paid off. Sheriff Rick Staley called it one of the most bizarre chases of his career, ending, as he put it, at the Green Roof Inn, his nickname for the county jail that he often refers to in a segment he calls Fugitive Friday Bingo. Merry Christmas Dirtbags. The Grinch has joined me today and it's time for Fugitive Friday Bingo, Super Bowl edition. Fugitive Bingo. Fugitive Bingo. Special edition of Fugitive Friday Bingo. New Year's Weekend Edition. Tammy faced. One count of fleeing law enforcement at high speed with wanton disregard. Five counts of principal to fire weapon or missile into a vehicle. One count of driving on a suspended license with a habitual modifier. Five counts of aggravated assault on a law enforcement officer, one count of petty theft, one count of grand theft auto, one count of reckless driving, and one count of attached vehicle tag not assigned. Her bond was set to $152,000. For all 16 charges, she faces a potential 35 years in prison. After initially pleading not guilty, she later pled Nolo Contendere, meaning she doesn't admit guilt, but agreed to be charged as if she were guilty. This was likely due to a plea deal. She was adjudicated guilty for three of her 16 charges and was sentenced one year and three months in prison, followed by three years of probation. She received 122 days of jail credit and must pay a fine of over $800. She has since been released, and records show she has completed her probation. Shane faced. One count of fleeing law enforcement with lights and sirens active, five counts of throwing deadly missiles, five counts of aggravated assault on a law enforcement officer, two counts of possession of a fire, or dangerous weapon as a convicted felon, one count of possession of drug paraphernalia, one count of driving on a suspended license, one count of grand theft auto, one count a petty theft, and two counts of reckless driving. His bail was set to $278,000. However, while awaiting trial, Shane started a fight with his cellmate over alleged stolen commissary, leaving the other inmate bloodied before officers ended the fight by tasering both of them. Shane was charged with battery on a detainee, and his bail was revoked. For all 20 charges, he faces 62 years in prison. Like Tammy, after initially pleading not guilty, he later pled Nolo Contendere, likely due to a plea deal. He was adjudicated guilty for eight of his 20 charges and was sentenced to eight years with fines totaling over $1,000. He was given 184 days of jail credit with no probation listed. In Florida, inmates typically serve 85% of their sentence with good behavior. In Shane's case, this would be a six-year. year and 10-month sentence, making his release date around April 2028. If he serves the full sentence, he will be released June 2030.

an example of their efficiency, but not without controversy.
The pursuit was unauthorized, and officers sped it over twice the limit without lights or sirens.
lights or sirens, frustrating some civilians. In their own footage release, FCSO edited out radio
traffic about the unauthorized chase. Conservative statistics cite that police pursuit fatalities
happen almost daily in the U.S. and often involve bystanders. The San Francisco Chronicle
provides some of the best resources regarding these statistics with an interactive website
that details some of the most dangerous states for police pursuit fatalities from 2017 to
to 2022. Georgia and Alabama takes the top two spots with over 20 deaths per one million people,
accounting for 10% of pursuit deaths in the whole nation. Florida, where this video takes place,
falls into 34th. Most pursuits in the U.S., regardless of the outcome, are subject to review by
the agency, and officers can receive coachings or discipline if found violating policy. Looking at
the 2017 Flagler Vehicle Apprehension Policy, this certainly seems to be the case,
But this information is not publicly accessible.

if the suspects committed a more serious crime after getting away.
